one_liner: Dart SDK's VM: adaptive JIT plus AOT compiler; beats PyPy 7.3.14 on all four plb2 tasks and LuaJIT 2.1 on three.
what_it_does: The Dart SDK contains the Dart VM (C++ runtime in runtime/), the shared Dart front end, the AOT pipeline behind `dart compile exe`, and the dart2js/dartdevc/Wasm web compilers. Running `dart file.dart` compiles source to a Kernel binary in a helper isolate and then JIT-executes it. You get speed by writing the program in Dart, not by swapping in a library: it does not run Python or Lua code. C++ hosts can embed the VM through runtime/include/dart_api.h, but that is niche compared with using the `dart` CLI or Flutter.
how_it_is_fast: In JIT mode, functions start in an unoptimizing compiler whose call sites use inline caches to record receiver types. Hot functions (and long loops, via on-stack replacement) are then recompiled in the background by an SSA-based optimizing compiler. It specializes code speculatively from that type feedback (inlining, range analysis, representation selection and unboxing, load forwarding, GVN, allocation sinking, linear-scan register allocation) and falls back to unoptimized code when an assumption breaks. AOT mode instead runs a whole-program type flow analysis (TFA) and devirtualizes calls only where it can prove the target, with no speculation. Memory is managed by a generational GC: a parallel semispace scavenger for the young generation and concurrent marking with mark-sweep/mark-compact for the old generation.
when_to_use: You are choosing a garbage-collected language for CPU-bound scripts or services, and Python or Lua under PyPy/LuaJIT is too slow. In plb2, Dart 3.2.4 was 1.8x to 2.7x faster than PyPy 7.3.14 on all four tasks.
Branchy integer or bit-twiddling code and small fixed arrays (plb2 nqueen and sudoku), where Dart was 1.5x and 3.7x faster than LuaJIT 2.1.
Pointer-heavy array-of-objects code (plb2 bedcov), where Dart (2.85 s) was 3.7x faster than LuaJIT (10.52 s).
Teams already on Flutter or Dart who want one language for app and backend, with the choice of JIT for development and AOT for deployment.
when_not_to_use: Dense float loops like matmul: Dart took 2.74 s against 1.14 s for OpenJDK 20 HotSpot and 0.76 s for Julia 1.10, and was 3% slower than LuaJIT.

Expecting AOT (`dart compile exe`) to match JIT on tight typed-data loops: issue #53513 (Uint32List graph traversal, 2.76 s JIT vs 15.22 s AOT) and open issue #62619 (scanline rasterizer, about 6.5x slower AOT on Dart 3.6.0) report AOT far slower.
When the fastest managed runtime is the goal: in the same plb2 table, .NET 8 (NativeAOT), Julia 1.10 and Bun 1.0.20 are faster than Dart on all four tasks.
Existing Python, Lua or JavaScript code you cannot rewrite; Dart is a separate language with its own libraries.
Lightweight embedding in a C++ application: the VM is large, built with Chromium depot_tools/GN, and the embedding API is not the main supported use.

integration.form: language toolchain (prebuilt SDK with `dart` CLI); the VM can also be built from source and embedded through runtime/include/dart_api.h
integration.dependencies: none to run the prebuilt SDK; building from source needs Python 3, Chromium depot_tools (gclient, GN, ninja) and Visual Studio 2017+ with the Windows 10 SDK on Windows
integration.min_toolchain: not documented for users; plb2 used Dart 3.2.4
integration.platforms: native code for x64, ARM and RISC-V on Linux, macOS and Windows (mobile through Flutter); JavaScript and WebAssembly for the web
integration.thread_safety: Isolate model: each isolate has its own state and usually its own mutator thread, and isolates in a group share a GC heap. Embedders attach one current isolate per thread (dart_api.h).

gotchas: Plb2's timed mode, resolved: commit 1e4d581 ('added makefile for dart compile exe', body 'this is slower...') shows the author found the AOT build slower. The '(JIT)' row therefore most likely times `dart file.dart`, not the Makefile's AOT executables. No run script is checked in.
The Dart matmul figure comes after a manual loop-hoisting commit (d704e27, 4.81 s to 2.74 s). The Lua, Python and Java ports hoist the same loop, so the comparison stays fair.

The plb2 Dart ports leave several parameters untyped (matmul(a, b), sudoku's _update(sr, sc, r, v) and solve(s_), `var i` in nqueen), so they run through dynamic dispatch. Dart's matmul gap to HotSpot may partly be port quality. This is not a correctness bug.

Wall-clock times include source-to-Kernel compilation in the kernel-service isolate and JIT warm-up. The sudoku run also prints every solution. These fixed costs are the same for all languages but weigh more on short runs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Dart over Julia or the .NET runtime when you want the Dart/Flutter ecosystem with both JIT and AOT deployment; for raw throughput, Julia and .NET beat it on every plb2 task. Pick it over Chez Scheme for bit-twiddling and matmul-style code (plb2 matmul 2.74 s vs Chez 9.5.8's 18.98 s), and over Graal.js only if you want a statically typed language rather than JavaScript.
verified_claims_summary: Plb2 (attractivechaos, hyperfine wall-clock on an Apple M1 MacBook Pro, January 2024) ran Dart 3.2.4 in JIT mode on four single-threaded tasks: nqueen 3.62 s, matmul 2.74 s, sudoku 3.24 s, bedcov 2.85 s. PyPy 7.3.14 took 6.91, 4.89, 8.82 and 6.27 s, so Dart was 1.78x to 2.72x faster (derived from page data). LuaJIT 2.1 took 5.31, 2.66, 4.48 and 10.52 s, so Dart won three of four and was 3% slower on matmul. Against OpenJDK 20 and Node 21 the results were mixed.
status_note: Very active (commit on 2026-10-06, 11.3k stars, BSD-3-Clause) and production-grade. You use it as a whole language toolchain rather than vendoring code, and the plb2 evidence is a single 2024 run of one author's ports.
